name: Los Angeles
tagline: Sun-drenched sprawl of cinema, ocean and reinvention.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Warm and dry most of the year, with spring and autumn the sweet spots; time it to jacaranda bloom, gray-whale migration or the awards-and-art season, and only the deep-summer smog and heat give pause.

ourTake.lede: Los Angeles punishes people who try to see all of it, pick a base, stay in its orbit, and accept that the drive between two points defines the day. The real texture is in the neighbourhoods and the food, not the tourist Walk of Fame, which you can skip entirely. Time in the canyons, on the coast at Malibu and in a good restaurant will tell you more about the city than any landmark.
ourTake.comeIf: You want beaches, studios and canyon-view hotels, and don't mind the drive everywhere.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a walkable city or a short flight.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Hotel Bel-Air, Dorchester Collection
credentials: World's 50 Best Hotels 2025 (No. 42, highest-ranked US hotel outside New York)
items.description: A twelve-acre canyon hideaway of swan lakes and secret gardens, Los Angeles at its most private.

items.name: The Beverly Hills Hotel, Dorchester Collection
items.description: The Pink Palace on Sunset since 1912, the definitive myth of Beverly Hills, still gracious.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Beverly Hills
items.description: A gleaming Pierre-Yves Rochon tower at Wilshire and Santa Monica, the marque's West Coast debut.

items.name: The Peninsula Beverly Hills
items.description: The group's flawless Californian house, the only Forbes Five-Star, AAA Five-Diamond hotel in Southern California, year after year.

items.name: Nobu Ryokan Malibu
credentials: Travel + Leisure, No. 1 Resort Hotel in the Continental US (World's Best)
items.description: A sixteen-room teak ryokan on Billionaire's Beach, the ocean at the foot of the bed.

items.name: The Maybourne Beverly Hills
items.description: The London group's Californian address, Claridge's polish, a block from Rodeo Drive.

items.name: Beverly Wilshire, Beverly Hills, A Four Seasons Hotel
items.description: A 1928 landmark at the foot of Rodeo Drive, grand-hotel bones, Four Seasons hands.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills
items.description: The surest hands in Los Angeles, a leafy, low-key garden hotel on Doheny Drive.

items.name: L'Ermitage Beverly Hills
items.description: The longest-tenured all-suite Forbes Five-Star hotel in the world, discreet, residential calm.

items.name: Chateau Marmont
items.description: The most storied hotel in Hollywood, a Loire-château fantasy above the Sunset Strip.

items.name: Pendry West Hollywood
items.description: A sleek Sunset Strip tower with a rooftop over the whole city, contemporary and buzzing.

items.name: The West Hollywood EDITION
items.description: Ian Schrager's white, garden-wrapped tower, quiet-luxury calm with a rooftop and a basement club.

items.name: Shutters on the Beach
items.description: A Cape-Cod beach house right on the sand, the ocean-side heart of Santa Monica.

items.name: Hotel Casa del Mar
items.description: A restored 1920s beach club on the sand, a grander, more romantic Santa Monica landmark.

items.name: Fairmont Miramar Hotel & Bungalows
items.description: A palm-shaded estate above the ocean bluffs, private bungalows and a century of history.

items.name: Sunset Tower Hotel
items.description: An Art Deco icon of the Sunset Strip, old-Hollywood glamour, discreetly kept alive.

items.name: The Georgian Hotel
items.description: A turquoise Art Deco jewel newly reborn on Ocean Avenue, glamour with an ocean view.

items.name: Santa Monica Proper Hotel
items.description: Kelly Wearstler's sun-bleached, texture-rich design hotel a block from the beach.

items.name: Downtown L.A. Proper Hotel
items.description: A 1920s landmark reborn as Kelly Wearstler's living museum, the coolest room downtown.

items.name: The Aster
items.description: A members'-club hotel in the heart of Hollywood, a rooftop pool and a fashionable crowd.

items.name: The Paramour Estate
items.description: A hilltop 1920s mansion turned private hotel, a Mediterranean villa above the city.

items.name: The Prospect Hollywood
items.description: An intimate, design-forward hideaway in the hills above Hollywood, small and personal.

items.name: Palihouse West Hollywood
items.description: A residential-style boutique house on a quiet WeHo street, apartment-living ease.

items.name: The Charlie
items.description: A cluster of English-cottage bungalows once home to Charlie Chaplin's circle, private and green.

items.name: The Getty Center
items.description: Richard Meier's travertine hilltop reached by a driverless tram, with European masters, Robert Irwin's Central Garden and a sweep of the whole basin from ocean to mountains. Admission is free (parking is paid); the light, the views and the calm make it an easy multi-generational half-day, and the restaurant is comfortable for a considered vegetarian lunch.

items.name: The Getty Villa
items.description: A re-imagined Roman country house above the Pacific Coast Highway, its antiquities set among reflecting pools, herb gardens and colonnades that look out to the sea. Free with a timed reservation; a private guide brings the Greek and Roman rooms alive for children, and the seaside setting pairs naturally with a Malibu drive.

items.name: Griffith Observatory
items.description: The 1935 Art Deco observatory on Mount Hollywood, with the Zeiss telescope, the Samuel Oschin Planetarium and the postcard view of the Hollywood Sign and the city grid at dusk. Admission and grounds are free; go at golden hour with a driver who knows the parking, and the planetarium show keeps every generation happy.

items.name: The Broad
items.description: Eli and Edythe Broad's contemporary collection behind a honeycomb 'veil' facade on Grand Avenue, home to Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Mirror Rooms and headline names from Koons to Basquiat. General admission is free but timed-entry books out; have your advisor secure slots ahead, especially for the Kusama room children love.

items.name: Walt Disney Concert Hall
items.description: Frank Gehry's billowing stainless-steel landmark, home of the LA Philharmonic and one of the most acoustically celebrated halls in the world. Even without a concert the free self-guided exterior and garden walk is worth it; for an evening, a box and a pre-show dinner nearby make a refined night out.

items.name: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
items.description: Renzo Piano's glass sphere on Wilshire, the film academy's own museum, with Oscars history, immersive galleries and the 1,000-seat Geffen Theater. The rooftop terrace over the Hollywood Hills is a highlight; a private tour suits movie-loving teenagers, and it sits a few steps from LACMA.

items.name: LACMA (Los Angeles County Museum of Art)
items.description: The largest art museum in the western United States, with Chris Burden's 'Urban Light' lamp-post forest out front and a deep South and Southeast Asian collection Indian families recognise instantly. A guided visit cuts the scale down to size; the campus flows straight into the Academy Museum and Petersen.

items.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum and Botanical Gardens
items.description: Henry Huntington's estate near Pasadena: a Gutenberg Bible and 'Blue Boy' indoors, and outdoors more than a dozen gardens including a serene Chinese garden and a formal Japanese garden with a tea house. Vast and peaceful, ideal for grandparents and children together; a golf-cart tour and a reserved tea are worth arranging.

items.name: Universal Studios Hollywood
items.description: A working studio and theme park in one, with the Studio Tour tram, the Wizarding World of Harry Potter and Super Nintendo World. The VIP Experience gives a private guide, back-lot access and front-of-line entry that spares a family the queues and heat.

items.name: Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood
items.description: A guided cart ride through real sound stages, back-lot streets and the Central Perk 'Friends' set, plus DC and Harry Potter props. Smaller and more intimate than a theme park; the private tour is a genuine behind-the-curtain treat for older children and film buffs.

items.name: Hollywood Walk of Fame & TCL Chinese Theatre
items.description: The terrazzo-and-brass stars along Hollywood Boulevard and the 1927 Chinese Theatre with its forecourt of hand and footprints. Best done briefly with a guide who knows the safe, worthwhile stretch; pair it with the Dolby Theatre (home of the Oscars) next door.

items.name: Runyon Canyon Park
items.description: The city's most social hike, a quick loop above the Hollywood flats with ridge-top views over the whole basin and a good chance of the sign. Short enough for a morning before the heat; a guide picks the right trailhead and the shaded route for a family walk.

items.name: Hollywood Sign hikes (Griffith Park trails)
items.description: Several routes lead to the sign's overlooks, from the gentler Griffith Park trails to the longer Mount Lee climb behind it. Go early with water and a driver on call; a knowledgeable guide keeps the pace right for mixed ages and finds the cleanest photo angle.

items.name: Santa Monica Pier & Beach
items.description: The classic Pacific pier with Pacific Park's Ferris wheel and the western end of Route 66, backed by a wide beach and the Third Street Promenade. Fun and easy for children; base an afternoon here and let the driver handle the notorious pier parking.

items.name: Venice Beach & Abbot Kinney Boulevard
items.description: The boardwalk's carnival of skaters, muscle beach and canals on one side, and Abbot Kinney's designer boutiques, coffee and independent dining on the other. The boardwalk is a quick curiosity; Abbot Kinney is the refined half, with good vegetarian and plant-forward spots.

items.name: Rodeo Drive & Beverly Hills
items.description: The two blocks of Rodeo with the flagship maisons, the curving cobbled Via Rodeo and the Beverly Wilshire on the corner. Private shopping appointments and a car-and-driver make it effortless; the tree-lined residential streets and Beverly Gardens Park reward a slow drive.

items.name: Petersen Automotive Museum
items.description: A ribboned red-and-steel building holding roughly 150 cars at a time, from Hollywood hero vehicles to hypercars, with 'The Vault' below of priceless rarities. The private Vault tour is the reason to come; a magnet for car-enthusiast fathers and sons.

items.name: The Grand Central Market
items.description: A 1917 food hall packed with stalls from old-line delis to modern chefs, a lively lunch stop in the heart of historic downtown. Plenty of vegetarian choices among the crowds; combine with the Bradbury Building and Angels Flight across the street.

items.name: Bradbury Building
items.description: An unassuming 1893 exterior hiding a light-filled Victorian atrium of wrought iron, marble stairs and cage lifts, familiar from 'Blade Runner'. A National Historic Landmark; the lobby is open to visitors briefly and rewards a five-minute detour off Broadway.

items.name: Angels Flight Railway
items.description: A tiny orange funicular, one of the oldest still running in the country, climbing Bunker Hill between Hill Street and California Plaza. A one-minute ride and a charming photo; it links Grand Central Market below to the Broad and Disney Hall above.

items.name: Olvera Street & El Pueblo de Los Angeles
items.description: The city's birthplace, a Mexican marketplace lane of adobe buildings, crafts and food beside the historic plaza church. A vivid, walkable slice of LA's origins; short and colourful, good for children and easy to fold into a downtown morning.

items.name: Watts Towers of Simon Rodia
items.description: Seventeen soaring towers of steel, mortar, tile and found glass, hand-built by one immigrant labourer over 33 years, now a State Historic Park. A National Historic Landmark and a moving folk-art marvel; visit with a guide and driver as part of a curated arts route.

items.name: Malibu beaches & Pacific Coast Highway drive
items.description: The cliff-hung coast road past Zuma, El Matador's sea stacks and the pier, some of the finest ocean driving in California. A chauffeured PCH day with lunch at a clifftop table is the graceful way to do it; El Matador's staircase suits the more adventurous.

items.name: Malibu wineries (Malibu Wine Country)
items.description: Hidden vineyards and tasting terraces in the Santa Monica Mountains behind the coast, some with resident giraffes and safari-style tours. A relaxed inland counterpoint to the beach; a private tasting and driver make an easy adults' afternoon.

items.name: Manhattan Beach
items.description: The most polished of the South Bay beach towns, a pier, a walkable downtown of boutiques and good restaurants and wide golden sand. Calmer and more upscale than Venice; a pleasant, family-friendly seaside base with strong dining.

items.name: Descanso Gardens
items.description: A 150-acre garden famed for its camellia forest under coast live oaks, a rose garden and a Japanese garden with a tea house. Quiet and shaded, lovely for grandparents; the seasonal light installations and the little train delight younger children.

items.name: The Los Angeles County Arboretum & Botanic Garden
items.description: A 127-acre garden of themed collections and roaming peacocks, wrapped around a historic Queen Anne cottage seen in old films. Space to wander for every age and an easy pairing with the Huntington nearby in the San Gabriel Valley.

items.name: Disneyland Resort
items.description: The original Disneyland and Disney California Adventure, roughly an hour south in Orange County, still the benchmark theme-park day. A private VIP tour guide handles the planning and skips the lines, turning a huge day into a smooth one for the whole family.

items.name: Six Flags Magic Mountain
items.description: The thrill-seeker's park north of the city, dense with world-record roller coasters. A day for teenagers chasing adrenaline; a driver for the 40-minute run up the I-5 keeps it simple.

items.name: Santa Catalina Island
items.description: A car-free Mediterranean-feeling island an hour by fast ferry from Long Beach or San Pedro, with the Avalon harbour, glass-bottom boats and clear coves. A genuine escape from the city; helicopter transfer and a golf-cart tour make it an effortless day out.

items.name: Palm Springs
items.description: The desert-modernist resort town about two hours east, with mid-century architecture, the Aerial Tramway up to alpine peaks and glossy resort dining. Better as an overnight, but a chauffeured architecture-and-spa day works; the tram is a hit with children.

items.name: Santa Barbara
items.description: The 'American Riviera' about 90 minutes up the coast, with a Spanish-colonial old mission, red-tiled State Street and wineries in the hills behind. A refined day or overnight; a driver frees everyone to enjoy the coast road and a long lunch.

items.name: Santa Ynez & Santa Barbara wine country
items.description: The rolling vineyards of 'Sideways' fame beyond Santa Barbara, with Los Olivos tasting rooms and grand estate wineries. A private driver is essential for a tasting day; the pace and scenery suit adults after a few busy city days.

items.name: Melrose Avenue & the Melrose Design District
items.description: From the graffiti-mural fashion stretch of Melrose to the high-end interiors and galleries of the Melrose and Pacific Design Center districts. Shopping and design browsing for grown-ups, with plenty of cafes; a driver stitches the scattered blocks together.

items.name: The Grove & Original Farmers Market
items.description: An open-air shopping street with a trolley beside the historic 1934 Farmers Market of food stalls and produce. Easy, walkable and central; the market's variety keeps children and vegetarians well fed between museum visits nearby.

items.name: The Museum of Contemporary Art (MOCA), Grand Avenue
items.description: The city's dedicated contemporary art museum on Grand Avenue, a compact, serious collection a short walk from The Broad and Disney Hall. A focused hour of Rothko, Rauschenberg and more; ideal to bundle into a downtown culture morning.

items.name: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County
items.description: Dinosaur halls, a dazzling gem-and-mineral vault and an immersive butterfly pavilion in Exposition Park. A reliable crowd-pleaser for children; sits beside the California Science Center in a single easy stop.

items.name: California Science Center
items.description: Home to the retired Space Shuttle Endeavour and hands-on science galleries, with free general admission. A must for space-struck children; a guide and reserved shuttle viewing avoid the busiest school-group hours.

items.name: The Original Farmers Market Fairfax and Canter's, Fairfax Village
items.description: The old Fairfax district around historic delis and the flagship Farmers Market, a taste of mid-century LA street life. A gentle walkable pocket; combine with LACMA and the Academy Museum a few minutes away.

items.name: Mulholland Drive scenic overlooks
items.description: The ridge road along the crest of the Santa Monica Mountains, with turnouts looking down over the city grid on one side and the Valley on the other. A short chauffeured sunset drive with two or three stops is a quiet luxury and a fine photo run.

items.name: Grand Park & the Civic Center
items.description: A terraced green ribbon of lawns and pink fountains running from City Hall up to the Music Center on Bunker Hill. A pleasant stroll linking the downtown cultural sights; City Hall's observation deck gives a free panoramic view.

items.name: Grammy Museum & L.A. Live
items.description: An interactive music museum in the L.A. Live entertainment complex beside Crypto.com Arena, with costumes, instruments and recording booths. Fun for music-loving teenagers; the surrounding plaza has easy dining before a game or concert.

items.name: Norton Simon Museum
items.description: A jewel-box museum in Pasadena with an exceptional European collection from Rembrandt to Degas plus a fine South Asian sculpture gallery. Small, uncrowded and beautifully hung; the Indian bronzes resonate with visiting families and it pairs with the Huntington.

items.name: Old Town Pasadena & the Gamble House
items.description: A handsome historic downtown of restored brick storefronts and dining, near the Gamble House, a masterpiece of American Arts-and-Crafts architecture. A relaxed shopping-and-architecture afternoon; the Gamble House interior tour rewards design lovers.

items.name: The Last Bookstore
items.description: A cavernous former bank turned bookshop with tunnels and arches made of books, one of downtown's most photographed interiors. A quick, atmospheric stop for readers and teenagers; steps from Grand Central Market and the Bradbury.

items.name: The Wallis Annenberg / Beverly Hills gardens & shopping stroll
items.description: The polished heart of Beverly Hills beyond Rodeo, with the Wallis Annenberg Center for the Performing Arts, Beverly Gardens Park and the lily pond. An unhurried, green counterpoint to shopping; suits an easy morning before lunch on Canon Drive.

items.name: Point Dume & the Malibu headlands
items.description: A dramatic bluff at the north end of Malibu with a short trail to whale-watching overlooks and a sheltered cove below. Wilder and quieter than the beaches south of it; a rewarding stop on a chauffeured Malibu day for the more active.

items.name: Providence
items.description: Michael Cimarusti's temple to seafood, Los Angeles's most decorated table, newly at three stars.

items.name: Somni
items.description: Aitor Zabala's intimate fourteen-seat counter, the first three-star ever awarded in LA County.

items.name: n/naka
items.description: Niki Nakayama's modern kaiseki, the most quietly revered tasting menu in Los Angeles.

items.name: Hayato
items.description: Brandon Go's eight-seat kaiseki hidden in the Arts District, Kyoto exactitude in Los Angeles.

items.name: Mélisse
items.description: Josiah Citrin's long-held two-star, contemporary French of great polish, on the Westside.

items.name: Kato
items.description: Jon Yao's Taiwanese-American tasting menu, personal, precise, and among the city's very best.

items.name: Mori Nozomi
items.description: An eight-seat sushi counter with fish flown from Japan multiple times a week, newly starred.

items.name: Nozawa Bar
items.description: A hidden ten-seat omakase behind Sugarfish, pure, classic edomae sushi.

items.name: Sushi Kaneyoshi
items.description: A basement counter of exacting edomae sushi, a serious, hushed omakase downtown.

items.name: Vespertine
items.description: Jordan Kahn's futuristic tasting menu in a Gehry-adjacent glass tower, dining as art installation.

items.name: Osteria Mozza
items.description: Nancy Silverton's Italian benchmark, the mozzarella bar and pasta that set the LA standard.

items.name: CUT by Wolfgang Puck
items.description: The most glamorous steakhouse in America, Wolfgang Puck's starred room in the Beverly Wilshire.

items.name: Orsa & Winston
items.description: Josef Centeno's intimate Italian-Japanese tasting counter, a quiet downtown gem.

items.name: Restaurant Ki
items.description: A ten-seat contemporary Korean counter, global technique on a Korean foundation.

items.name: Meteora
items.description: Jordan Kahn's fire-driven, live-flame cooking, theatrical, primal, singular.

items.name: Kali
items.description: Kevin Meehan's seasonal Californian cooking, refined, ingredient-led, unshowy.

items.name: Shin Sushi
items.description: A Valley omakase counter of great purity, quiet mastery away from the Westside crowds.

items.name: Kojima
items.description: An intimate sushi counter on Sawtelle's Japantown strip, refined and personal.

items.name: Miura
items.description: A precise Japanese counter that earned its star with quiet, seasonal craft.

items.name: Pasta | Bar
items.description: An intimate Italian tasting counter in the Valley, pasta as a tasting menu.

items.name: Holbox
items.description: Gilberto Cetina's Yucatán seafood counter, ceviches and tostadas good enough for a star.

items.name: Pijja Palace
items.description: An Indian-American sports bar that became LA's most loved crossover, tandoori spaghetti and cricket on the screens.

items.name: Jitlada
items.description: The fiery southern-Thai institution of LA's Thai Town, decades deep and still unrivalled.

items.name: Pine & Crane
items.description: Bright, modern Taiwanese home cooking in an airy room, fresh, fast, beloved.

items.name: Pizzeria Bianco
items.description: Chris Bianco's LA outpost, widely called the best pizza in America, now downtown.

items.name: Pizzeria Mozza
items.description: Nancy Silverton and Mario Batali's blistered-crust pizzas, the room that reset LA pizza.

items.name: Pizzana
items.description: Daniele Uditi's neo-Neapolitan pizza, soft, charred, and quietly perfect.

items.name: Rossoblu
items.description: Steve Samson's Bolognese cooking, handmade pasta and a warm, cavernous downtown room.

items.name: Cobi's
items.description: Bright, inventive Southeast-Asian cooking in a leafy garden room, fresh and easy to love.

items.name: Colapasta
items.description: A small, sincere pasta room doing handmade Italian classics on the Westside.

items.name: Sea Harbour Seafood Restaurant
items.description: Cantonese dim sum of real refinement, a San Gabriel Valley institution, fairly priced.

items.name: The Tower Bar, Sunset Tower Hotel
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN One-Key hotel, a genuine Sunset Strip institution
items.description: Old-Hollywood glamour in Bugsy Siegel's former apartment, the most storied nightcap on the Strip.

items.name: Bar Marmont / Chateau Marmont
credentials: Inside a MICHELIN Two-Key hotel, a Hollywood institution
items.description: A drink in the most legendary hotel in Hollywood, discreet, dimly lit, endlessly mythologised.

items.name: The Polo Lounge, The Beverly Hills Hotel
credentials: Inside a Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN Three-Key hotel, a global institution
items.description: The power-lunch and nightcap of Beverly Hills since 1941, pink banquettes under the tropical garden.

items.name: Mírate
credentials: North America's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 12), highest LA entry
items.description: A rooftop mezcal-and-agave temple over Los Feliz, the highest-ranked bar in Los Angeles.

items.name: Thunderbolt
items.description: A breezy, boundary-pushing SoCal cocktail bar, laboratory technique with a Southern soul.

items.name: Death & Co Los Angeles
items.description: The New York cocktail institution's LA home, impeccable drinks in the Arts District.

items.name: Genever
items.description: A Filipina-run gin bar of real character, one of the city's most distinctive drinking rooms.

items.name: Dante Beverly Hills, The Maybourne
credentials: An outpost of a former World's Best Bar (Dante), atop a Forbes 5-Star hotel
items.description: The New York World's-Best bar transplanted to a Maybourne rooftop, negronis with a view.

items.name: Bar Next Door
items.description: A speakeasy-style hideaway beneath a restaurant, intimate, low-lit, seriously made drinks.

plan.heading: 4 days in Los Angeles, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and settle into a garden suite at the Hotel Bel-Air, breakfast under the sycamores.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Getty Center in the afternoon, the gardens, the collection, the view down to the ocean.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at n/naka in Palms, the kaiseki menu, booked far ahead.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Drive the coast to Malibu, a morning at El Matador beach before it fills.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Nobu Malibu over the water, then the Getty Villa's antiquities.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset drinks in Santa Monica, dinner at Providence in Hollywood.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Broad and its Yayoi Kusama rooms, booked at opening.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Design and galleries along Melrose and the Arts District, lunch at Bestia.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A show at the Hollywood Bowl in season, or dinner at Vespertine.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A morning hike in Runyon Canyon or a quiet drive through Mulholland's viewpoints.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch in Beverly Hills and a last hour on Rodeo before the airport.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Evening flight, or a late table at Republique if the timing holds.

items.name: Beverly Hills
items.description: Manicured and central to the Westside, walking distance to Rodeo Drive, the safe, polished base for first-timers.

items.name: Santa Monica / Venice
items.description: Beach-adjacent and walkable by LA standards; Santa Monica for ease, Venice for edge and design.

items.name: West Hollywood
items.description: Design hotels, nightlife and the Sunset Strip, for travellers who want to be out, not by the sand.

events.name: Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival
events.note: Two hours east in Indio; the marquee festival that empties fashionable LA into the desert.

events.name: Academy Awards
events.note: The ceremony itself is closed, but the city's energy, parties and restaurant scene peak around Oscars weekend.

events.name: ASICS Los Angeles Marathon
events.note: The Stadium-to-the-Stars course runs from Dodger Stadium to Century City, closing swathes of the city for a morning.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Base yourself in Beverly Hills or Bel-Air for privacy and proximity, or Malibu for the coast; the ESTA is required in advance, restaurant and Nobu-tier reservations should be locked early, and build generous buffers around traffic for anything time-sensitive.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Land at LAX, or Van Nuys/Burbank if flying private, and take a pre-arranged chauffeured SUV, as this is a city where the car is the front door.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver is essential; distances are large, parking is a nuisance, and a good driver who knows the canyons and traffic patterns is worth more than any app.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: US eSIM works flawlessly citywide; hotel and venue Wi-Fi is strong throughout.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: US dollar; cards and mobile pay everywhere, cash almost unnecessary; tip ~20% dining and $2–5 for valet and bell service.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: March-May and September-November are the sweet spots, warm and dry without summer crowds; skip the June gloom of overcast mornings and the hottest, smoggiest stretch of late summer.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; cleanest routings are via San Francisco on Air India or via a Gulf hub (Emirates via Dubai, Qatar via Doha) or London, roughly 18-20 hours door to door in J or F. Emirates first class via Dubai is the most comfortable single-connection option.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; ESTA or US visa required in advance. LA is safe in the districts a UHNI traveller frequents; a car and driver is the norm given the distances. Tap water is safe.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy and Jain is workable, with a large Indian community in Artesia and strong plant-based dining citywide. Consider the vegetarian tasting menus in the city or the Indian restaurants of Artesia's Little India.
